subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which two sociologists put forward the functionalist theory that social stratification is necessary and beneficial for society?
questions.explain: Davis and Moore (1945) argued stratification is functional because it ensures the most important roles are filled by the most talented people.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, the class that owns the means of production is known as the:
questions.explain: Marx called the owners of the means of production the bourgeoisie, who exploit the working-class proletariat.

questions.q: According to functionalists such as Davis and Moore, why does social stratification exist?
options: It ensures the most important roles are filled by the most talented people
It allows the ruling class to exploit the workers
It reflects only differences in status and honour
It traps the poor in a cycle of deprivation
questions.explain: Functionalists see unequal rewards as a way of motivating the most able people to train for and fill society's most important positions.

questions.q: Weber argued that stratification is based on three dimensions: social class, status and:
questions.explain: Weber saw stratification as shaped by three factors: class (economic position), status (social honour) and party (power).

questions.q: In Marxist theory, 'false consciousness' refers to:
options: the workers not realising they are being exploited by the ruling class
the ruling class being unaware of their own power
workers having a clear awareness of class conflict
the process of moving up the class system
questions.explain: False consciousness is when the proletariat fail to recognise their exploitation, which prevents them from challenging capitalism.

questions.q: A hospital pays its surgeons far more than its cleaners, arguing that surgery requires rare talent and years of training. Which theory best explains this pay gap?
questions.explain: Functionalists (Davis and Moore) argue higher rewards are justified for functionally important roles that require scarce talent and training.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the difference between wealth and income?
options: Wealth is the total value of assets a person owns, while income is money received regularly such as wages
Income is the value of property owned, while wealth is money spent each week
Wealth and income mean exactly the same thing
Income refers only to savings, while wealth refers only to benefits
questions.explain: Wealth is a stock of assets (property, savings, shares), whereas income is a flow of money such as wages, salaries or benefits.

questions.q: Which of the following would be counted as income rather than wealth?
options: A house that is owned outright
questions.explain: A salary is money received regularly, so it is income; property, shares and savings are assets and therefore wealth.

questions.q: The official classification used to measure social class in Britain today is the:
questions.explain: The NS-SEC is the official measure of social class in Britain, based largely on a person's occupation.

questions.q: A status that a person is born with and cannot change is described as:
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed at birth (such as being born into royalty), whereas achieved status is earned through a person's own efforts.

questions.q: Amara owns two houses, a large share portfolio and substantial savings. These assets are best described as her:
questions.explain: Property, shares and savings are accumulated assets, which is what sociologists mean by wealth.

questions.q: The sociologist most associated with the concept of relative poverty in Britain is:
questions.explain: Peter Townsend developed the idea of relative poverty, arguing that poverty means being unable to share in the living standards of one's society.

questions.q: Absolute poverty is best defined as:
options: lacking the basic necessities needed to survive, such as food, shelter and clothing
being poorer than most other people in your society
being unable to afford luxuries such as holidays
earning slightly less than the national average wage
questions.explain: Absolute poverty means lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, regardless of the standards of the wider society.

questions.q: Charles Murray used which term to describe a group at the bottom of society seen as detached from mainstream values?
questions.explain: Murray argued that a dependent 'underclass' had developed, holding values that differed from the rest of society.

questions.q: The 'culture of poverty' theory, associated with Oscar Lewis, argues that:
options: the poor develop values and attitudes that keep them trapped in poverty
poverty is caused entirely by the low wages set by employers
poverty can be measured only in absolute terms
the welfare state has completely abolished poverty
questions.explain: The culture of poverty thesis suggests the poor pass on fatalistic values that make it harder to escape poverty.

questions.q: The Okafor family can afford food and rent but cannot afford a family holiday, a computer or days out that most families in Britain enjoy. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Relative poverty means being unable to afford the goods and activities regarded as normal by most people in that society.

questions.q: Which 1942 report laid the foundations of the modern welfare state by identifying 'five giant evils'?
questions.explain: The Beveridge Report (1942) identified five giants - want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness - and shaped the post-war welfare state.

questions.q: In Weberian sociology, 'life chances' refers to:
options: a person's chances of obtaining the things valued in their society, such as good health and education
the number of years a person is expected to live
the chance of winning promotion at work
the likelihood of joining a political party
questions.explain: Weber used 'life chances' to describe a person's opportunities to gain valued things like good housing, health and education.

questions.q: Weber identified three types of authority: charismatic, traditional and:
questions.explain: Weber's three types of legitimate authority are charismatic, traditional and rational-legal (based on formal rules and laws).

questions.q: Ben's parents were manual factory workers, but Ben trained as a lawyer and now works in a senior professional role. Ben's change in class position is an example of:
questions.explain: Moving to a higher class position than one's parents is upward (intergenerational) social mobility, which is possible in an open society.

specSource: AQA GCSE Sociology (8192) specification; The Sociology of Social Stratification
